slides: Welcome to the lecture on the Bloch Conjecture and its Generalisations. In this session, we investigate the structure of Chow groups of zero-cycles for surfaces with geometric genus zero. We study Godeaux surfaces, outline general filtrations on Chow groups such as the Saito filtration, and examine Beauville's decomposition and Fourier transforms on abelian varieties.

We establish our Bloch operator contract, laying out the logical flow of our study. We examine surfaces with pg=0, establish the conjectural Bloch-Beilinson and Saito filtration towers on Chow groups, and use the Fourier transform to diagonalize Pontryagin product structures on abelian varieties.

The classical Bloch conjecture asserts that if a smooth projective surface has geometric genus zero, then its degree-zero Chow group is representable, forcing it to vanish if the Albanese variety is trivial. We explore the Godeaux surface as a key test case with non-trivial fundamental group, illustrating how Bloch's conjecture acts on surfaces with non-trivial topology.

We study filtrations on Chow groups, focusing on the conjectural Bloch-Beilinson filtration and the Saito filtration. These filtrations organize cycles into graded towers, where each successive step loses complex information in a controlled way, allowing us to study algebraic cycles layer by layer.

The generalised Bloch conjecture extends these ideas to higher-dimensional varieties. It proposes that if specific Hodge cohorts vanish, then specific stages of the Chow filtration must also collapse. This sets up a deep, general duality between transcendental Hodge theory and algebraic cycle groups.

We introduce abelian varieties and the Pontryagin product. Unlike the standard intersection product which acts as a ring multiplication, the Pontryagin product is defined by the addition map on the variety, behaving like a group algebra convolution. We trace how these two product operations interact.

The Fourier transform on Chow groups, pioneered by Beauville, diagonalizes the Pontryagin product, decomposing the Chow ring of an abelian variety into a direct sum of eigenspaces under the scaling map. This provides an elegant classification of cycles, mirroring classical Fourier analysis.

We verify our algebraic and Fourier theorems using the chapter's numerical model. Our finite Fourier transform is unitary after normalization, with a residual under 1e-15, and the Pontryagin convolution diagonalizes perfectly. Our toy Hodge ledger exhibits perfect symmetry with middle Betti number six and zero geometric genus.

In summary, Chapter 11 completes our study of algebraic cycles by presenting the Bloch conjecture as a filtration story. When working with cycles on surfaces or abelian varieties, always maintain our ledger: verify the genus assumptions, trace the Pontryagin and intersection maps, and record the surviving invariants.
